about: The term registry: the one home of every plain definition the public docs use.
glossary.html is generated from it, and so are the definitions the Plain English decoder shows.
terms_test.go holds every page in enforced_pages to one rule: the first use of a registered term
on that page is a marked definition (<dfn> in HTML, <dfn>*term*</dfn> in markdown) or a link to
its glossary entry. A term marked assumed is one the reader is expected to know; it is listed in
the glossary but its first use is not enforced. A term that names a chapter gets a link to
that chapter of glossary.html from its A to Z entry. After editing this file, run
go test ./docs/trainers -run TestGeneratedBlocks -update to regenerate the pages built from it.

terms.definition: The daemon's capacity check just before a run starts: it reserves a slot within the concurrency and memory limits, or refuses at once instead of queueing.
Cryptographic proof, usually rooted in the hardware, of exactly what software a machine is running; plimsoll's isolation tiers are evidence it collected, not attestation.
An overloaded service telling its callers to slow down, and the callers doing so.
The part of plimsoll that makes API calls for sandboxed code: it checks each call against the grant, attaches the credential itself, and counts the calls, so the code never sees the credential.
A power-supply circuit that turns a higher DC voltage into a lower one by switching it on and off many times a second.
A cart on a rail with a pole hinged on top; the task is to push the cart left and right so the pole stays upright.
The Linux kernel feature that caps and counts the memory, CPU time and number of processes a group of processes may use.
A switch in the broker that, after the API answers 429 (too many requests) or 503 (unavailable), stops forwarding calls for a cooldown so the API can recover.
Letting an AI agent write a short program that calls an API and run it in a sandbox, instead of calling one tool per step.
An RPC framework whose Go library serves protobuf-defined procedures over ordinary HTTP; plimsolld and its Go client use it.
A process started with its own view of files, network and other processes, while still sharing the host's operating-system kernel.
Identified by a digest of its own content, so the identifier can never later point at different content.
The formula a controller applies at each tick to turn its measurements into an action.
A program that reads a system's state at every tick and decides how to push it, for example to keep a pole balanced on a cart.
A network policy that blocks every connection unless a rule explicitly allows it.
A SHA-256 hash of some content, used as its name: the same digest always means the same bytes.
Handing a checked request to the provider so the code starts running; a request refused before dispatch ran nothing.
Docker's hosted service that runs each sandbox as a microVM on Docker-managed machines; the dockercloud provider starts one per run and is billed per use.
Dead Simple Signing Envelope: a small standard format that wraps a payload together with its signatures.
A hosted service that runs code in Firecracker microVMs; the e2b provider starts one per run and is billed per use.
Network traffic leaving the sandbox; plimsoll runs have none, apart from the single path a grant opens to the broker.
A bug that lets code inside a sandbox act outside it.
To refuse, rather than allow, when a check cannot be completed or a required setting is missing.
Calling an API once per item of a list instead of once for the whole list; also called the N+1 pattern.
A SHA-256 hash that stands for some content: equal fingerprints mean identical bytes, and any change gives a different fingerprint.
The open-source virtual machine monitor, built by AWS, that starts and runs microVMs; E2B runs every sandbox on it.
The weakest isolation tier a request will accept; if the daemon's provider is weaker, the request is refused and nothing runs.
Go's official vulnerability scanner, which reports known vulnerabilities only in code your program actually calls.
Permission, attached to one run, for its code to call listed routes of one HTTP API through the broker; a run without a grant has no network at all.
A grant stored on the server under a name, holding the API's address, the allowed routes, the callers allowed to use it and how its credential is made; a caller sends only the name.
The HTTPS endpoint, served by the plimsoll daemon, that is the only address a microVM run with a grant may reach; it checks the run's guard credential and hands each call to the broker.
The code running inside a sandbox, seen from the host machine that runs it.

Google's open-source stand-in kernel, written in Go and running as an ordinary program, that handles almost every request a container's code makes itself and uses only a short, locked-down list of real kernel calls.
The startup setting PLIMSOLL_HARDENED=1, under which the daemon refuses to start unless every production safeguard is configured.
Processor support for running several virtual machines on one computer, each with its own kernel, kept apart by the CPU itself.
A program outside the daemon that drives runs and checks their results; plimsoll's attest harness signs run records and verifies them later.
The program that runs virtual machines and keeps them apart, so code that breaks out of a virtual machine still has to break the hypervisor.
A standard format for signed statements about software; plimsoll's harness signs each run record as an in-toto statement inside a DSSE envelope.

How strong the wall around a run is, reported as one of four levels, weakest first: process, container, kernel, vm; the disabled provider reports none, and a provider that has not yet checked its runtime reports unknown.
An open-source container runtime that starts a small virtual machine, with its own kernel, for each sandbox, so the processor's virtualization features keep sandboxes apart.
The core part of the operating system that talks to the hardware and does every file, network and memory operation on every program's behalf.
The mark painted on a ship's hull showing how low it may safely sit in the water, where anyone can check it; plimsoll is named after it.
A file that lists what something contains, such as the files in a release or the layers of a container image.
Model Context Protocol: the open standard an AI application uses to offer tools, such as a run-code tool, to a language model.
A small virtual machine with its own kernel, started for one run and destroyed after it.
To create a fresh credential for one run, ideally short-lived and limited to that run's routes, so a stolen copy is soon useless.
Running a compiled simulator that is baked into a docker image, once for each row of a table of parameters.
A Linux kernel feature that controls what a program can see: its own files, its own process list, its own network.
Running a virtual machine inside another virtual machine; not every cloud server allows it.
A mount option that stops the kernel from running any program stored on that filesystem.
A mount option that stops a program on that filesystem from gaining extra privileges through its set-user-ID bit.

The program Docker hands a container to, which builds the walls around it, such as runc (the default), runsc (gVisor) or Kata Containers; OCI, the Open Container Initiative, wrote the standard it follows, so one can replace another without changing the image.
NVIDIA OpenShell, an agent sandbox runtime whose gateway server creates and deletes sandboxes on request; the openshell provider asks a gateway for one sandbox per run.
The example that tests an agent-written controller by running it against a simulated cart-pole inside the sandbox and fingerprinting what happens.
Fixed to one exact version, usually by digest, so it changes only when someone edits the pin.

The configuration check a provider runs at startup and on each readiness poll: for docker it confirms the images and the runtime exist; for openshell it asks the gateway which driver it runs; for e2b and dockercloud it checks settings only.
The authenticated identity a request comes from; in plimsolld, the caller id listed in the clients file, or static for the one caller of a shared PLIMSOLL_TOKEN.
One running program, with its own memory and its own permissions.
Protocol Buffers: Google's schema-defined binary format for messages, which plimsoll uses for its RPC requests and responses.

A number every request carries to name the protocol version it speaks; a daemon serving a different version refuses the request before reading it, rather than running it without fields it does not know.
A record of where an artifact came from and how it was built, kept so that someone else can check it.
The backend that actually runs the code; each daemon uses exactly one: wasm, docker, e2b, dockercloud, openshell, or disabled, which runs nothing and is what an unset SANDBOX_PROVIDER selects.
A small JavaScript engine; plimsoll embeds a build of it, compiled to WebAssembly, for its wasm provider.
Remote procedure call: one program sending a request to another over the network and getting an answer back.

The statement plimsolld attaches to every answered run: SHA-256 digests of the request and the result, the isolation evidence, and the start and end times; the official client recomputes the digests and rejects a mismatch.
Docker's default container runtime, and usually Kubernetes's too, which separates containers with the kernel's namespaces and cgroups while they all share the host's kernel.
gVisor's container runtime: the program docker calls instead of runc to start a container under gVisor.
The Kubernetes setting that chooses which container runtime, such as gVisor's runsc, runs a pod.
A place where code runs with something stopping it from reaching the rest of the machine.
A Linux kernel feature that limits which system calls a process may make; plimsoll ships a profile listing the calls its containers may use.

One sandbox kept open for many calls: files one call writes are there for the next, but no process outlives the call that started it, except the interpreter (a Python or Node.js process) the session keeps for its cells.
To refuse extra work at once, instead of queueing it, when a limit is reached.
Everything outside your own code that ends up in what you run: dependencies, base images, build tools, and the people and servers that publish them.
A request from a program to the operating-system kernel, such as opening a file, starting a process or opening a network connection.
Trusted computing base: the code that has to be correct for a security promise to hold, so a bug anywhere in it can break the promise.
The list of attackers and attacks a system is designed to hold out against.
One fixed time step of a simulation; the cart-pole examples take 10 ms per tick, so 100 ticks make one simulated second.
A filesystem held in memory, with a size limit set when it is mounted; its contents disappear when the container stops.
A rate limit that allows short bursts: each caller's allowance refills at a steady rate and each run spends one unit of it.
The full record of a simulation run: every state at every tick, in order.
A hosted job runner for TypeScript whose durable chat agents can sleep between messages; the trigger-chat example gives one an executeCode tool backed by plimsoll.
A complete computer simulated in software, with its own kernel, kept apart from other virtual machines by the processor's virtualization features.
A WebAssembly runtime written in pure Go; plimsoll uses it to run QuickJS inside the daemon with a hard memory cap.
A portable bytecode format that runs inside a host program, which decides everything the code can reach: no files, network or system calls unless the host provides them.
